profiles.meeting_scenario: A lab brainstorming meeting between a faculty advisor and a senior PhD student who are planning an updated survey/tutorial paper on neural machine reading comprehension for a journal special issue and a related lab seminar. The context is that both want to synthesize methods and trends in MRC, but they need to quickly decide the framing, section structure, and what kinds of materials belong in the main paper versus supporting resources. The agenda is to brainstorm how to organize the survey around task definitions, datasets, architecture, and emerging trends, and to identify a workable division of labor for an outline. The expected outcome is a shared high-level plan for the survey's framing, including candidate sections, a dataset summary table, an architecture overview figure, and an initial literature-screening approach.

members.name: Dr. Lina Zhou
members.role: Associate Professor and NLP Lab PI
members.expertise: Question answering, evaluation methodology, survey synthesis
members.background: Lina has worked on extractive and multi-hop QA since the pre-transformer era and has previously coauthored a survey on text understanding benchmarks; she is experienced at turning broad areas into compact conceptual taxonomies.
members.private_state: She wants a survey that is publishable within one academic term, reads as disciplined rather than sprawling, and is clearly distinct from generic LLM-overview articles; she is quietly worried that an overly broad scope will become impossible to finish and hard to position.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'recent trends' in neural MRC, they usually mean late-stage developments within the established MRC literature, with LLM-based work mentioned as an extension rather than the center of gravity.
A 'representative datasets' table in the main text should be compact, with one or two canonical datasets per task family and niche variants moved to an appendix or companion spreadsheet.
A 'comprehensive survey' is comprehensive if the taxonomy and historical through-line are conceptually complete, even if many incremental papers are omitted.

The default architecture readers expect for neural MRC is the classic reader pipeline centered on passage encoding, interaction/attention, and answer prediction, with newer components added as variants.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: LLM-based question answering, multilingual benchmarks, retrieval-augmented systems
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's QA benchmark tracker and has recently published on multilingual and retrieval-augmented reading comprehension; he is comfortable with large literature maps and cross-benchmark comparisons.
members.private_state: He wants the project to foreground post-2021 developments so his current line of work is visible in the paper, and he hopes to shape the survey into a resource that other researchers will use as a near-complete entry point into the area.
hidden_assumptions: When researchers now say 'recent trends' in MRC, they primarily mean instruction-tuned LLMs, retrieval augmentation, long-context models, and cross-lingual transfer.

A 'representative datasets' summary should visibly cover multilingual, domain-specific, conversational, and multi-hop settings in the main text because otherwise the field will look artificially narrow.
A 'comprehensive survey' should function as a practical literature map, so most benchmark-setting or highly cited variants in each subarea should be listed somewhere prominent.
The architecture overview that best represents current MRC work is a retriever-reader-generator style stack, possibly with reranking or tool use, not just a classic span-prediction reader.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly agree to include a section on 'recent trends' in neural MRC.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means developments that emerged within the established neural MRC line of work, such as multi-hop reasoning, unanswerable questions, conversational QA, and perhaps a brief bridge to LLM-era work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the post-2021 landscape, especially instruction-tuned LLMs, retrieval-augmented QA, long-context prompting, and multilingual transfer as the main trend story.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds naturally shared, and both can name plausible examples without contradiction; each hears the other's examples as compatible extensions rather than evidence of a different time horizon and center of gravity.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in a 'representative datasets' table
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the paper should have a 'representative datasets' table.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the main paper will show a concise table with only flagship datasets for each major task family, while specialized multilingual or domain-specific benchmarks are supplementary material.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the main comparative table itself should include multilingual, biomedical, conversational, and other non-canonical benchmarks so readers immediately see the breadth of the field.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both view the phrase 'representative datasets' as obviously sensible, but neither states the boundary between main-text essentials and supplementary breadth because that boundary feels like a formatting detail rather than a conceptual disagreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on writing a 'comprehensive survey' that will 'cover the area well'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks comprehensiveness means a clean taxonomy, historical arc, and citation of seminal or category-defining papers, even if many iterative variants are excluded.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks comprehensiveness means readers should be able to recover nearly the full active literature of each subarea, including benchmark-shifting and highly cited variants, not just the canonical exemplars.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the meeting is framed as brainstorming rather than execution planning, neither person operationalizes the criterion with counts or inclusion rules; 'comprehensive' functions as a flattering umbrella term that masks different thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'architecture overview figure' they are referring to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the survey should include 'the architecture overview figure' for neural MRC.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is picturing a standard reader diagram centered on embedding/encoding, context-question interaction, modeling, and answer prediction, suitable for classic extractive MRC.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is picturing a modern stack with retrieval, reranking, reading/generation, and possibly instruction tuning or external tools, intended to represent present-day systems.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They speak as though there is one obvious placeholder figure to draft later, and each assumes the other is invoking the same canonical mental image because both figures can plausibly be called 'the general architecture of MRC'.

turns.inner_thought: This special issue is a good chance, but only if we keep the scope disciplined enough to finish in one term. For me, a comprehensive survey means a clean taxonomy of neural MRC, a clear historical through-line from classic extractive setups through later task variants, and enough seminal papers to define each category. I do not want this to drift into a generic everything-about-LLMs piece or a giant catalog that's impossible to polish.
turns.utterance: I think we have a real opportunity here to do a strong survey-tutorial piece on neural MRC for the special issue. What I'd like today is to settle on a framing that feels comprehensive and covers the area well, but still reads cleanly rather than as a giant laundry list.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if we position this right, it can become the resource people actually use. To me, recent trends are the real story now: instruction-tuned systems, retrieval augmentation, long-context setups, multilingual transfer, all the things that changed the field after 2021. And the representative datasets table should show breadth in the main paper so readers immediately see that MRC is not just a couple of English span benchmarks.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. My instinct would be to center it around methods, representative datasets, and a solid section on recent trends so it feels current, not just retrospective. That way the paper can work both as a survey and as an entry point for people coming into the area now.

turns.inner_thought: Task families first is the safest backbone: extractive, abstractive, multi-hop, conversational, maybe unanswerable and domain-shifted settings as branches. The representative datasets table should anchor those sections without eating pages; one or two canonical datasets per family in the main text, anything more specialized can go elsewhere. If we avoid becoming a benchmark catalog, the paper will stay publishable and readable.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I wonder if the most stable backbone is to organize by task family first, then use a representative datasets table to anchor each section. I'd prefer not to let the paper turn into a benchmark catalog, but the table could keep the discussion concrete.

turns.inner_thought: I like task families, but the table has to visibly include multilingual, conversational, biomedical, and other domain-specific settings in the main text, otherwise readers will assume the survey is narrower than it is. Those are exactly where recent trends are most apparent. If the paper is supposed to be broadly useful, people should be able to scan one table and see the field's real spread.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For the representative datasets table, I do think we should make room for multilingual, conversational, and domain-specific settings, because that helps show where recent trends are heading and gives the sections some visible breadth.

turns.inner_thought: We also need the familiar architectural story early: passage and question encoding, interaction or attention, modeling layers, answer prediction. That's the architecture overview figure readers will expect in a neural MRC survey. Later model changes can be shown as extensions on top of that core picture, which preserves the historical line instead of replacing it.
turns.utterance: We should probably also put the architecture overview figure fairly early in the paper. I imagine starting from the standard reader pipeline and then noting how later models extend it, so readers have a common frame before we branch into the task sections.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—the architecture overview figure can be the modern end-to-end stack: retrieval up front, maybe reranking, then reading or generation, with the current training style sitting across the system. That would make the survey feel up to date and tie naturally into recent trends. I assume Lina means the same general figure, just introduced from a slightly earlier angle.
turns.utterance: Yes, that would work well. The architecture overview figure can then naturally absorb the additional modules people now expect, so it connects the earlier framing to current neural MRC systems without needing a separate conceptual reset later.

turns.inner_thought: I need to set an inclusion norm now before this balloons. Comprehensive should not mean chasing every minor leaderboard iteration. We should privilege seminal and category-defining papers, maybe a few especially influential follow-ons, and let the taxonomy do the work. Otherwise we'll never finish, and the narrative will get swamped by paper-by-paper enumeration.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want us to be intentional about: if we're aiming for a comprehensive survey, I think we should prioritize seminal and category-defining papers, rather than trying to summarize every leaderboard-era variant. We'll cover the area well if the structure is clear and the citations are well chosen.

turns.inner_thought: I can make that happen by pulling from the benchmark tracker, but in my mind a comprehensive literature map should still capture most of the influential variants in each subarea, not just the canonical starting points. If I assemble a broad map first, we can always compress later. I assume Lina also wants something fairly full, just organized carefully.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I can pull together a comprehensive literature map from the benchmark tracker, so for each task bucket we at least have the main influential variants in view as we decide what belongs in the write-up.

turns.inner_thought: So the deliverable in my head is a compact main paper: task-family sections, a clean representative datasets table, one architecture overview figure built around the classic reader story, and a final section on recent trends and open problems that bridges to newer work without letting it dominate. If we keep the main text tight, supplementary material can absorb anything expansive.
turns.utterance: Great. Then the shape I'm seeing is a compact main paper with task definitions up front, a clean representative datasets table, one architecture overview figure, and a final section on recent trends plus open problems. That should give us something coherent for the journal piece and also easy to reuse for the seminar.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll draft the dataset summary with visible breadth, sketch the architecture overview figure in the modern system style, and cluster papers under recent trends with the post-2021 landscape as the backbone. If I bring a rich enough draft, we can trim if needed, but at least the paper will start from a near-complete picture.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll take a first pass at the dataset summary and the architecture materials in that framing, and I'll also cluster papers for the recent trends section so we have something concrete to react to at the next meeting.
